explanation: To 'beggar description' means to be so extreme or extraordinary that words are inadequate to describe it (Shakespeare, Antony and Cleopatra). The 'beggar' here is a verb meaning 'to impoverish/outstrip', so the literal readings about beggars are traps.

'Alive and kicking' means still living and in good health and spirits, often said of someone assumed to be dead or finished. The literal image is of a kicking baby, but the idiom is about vigour, not infants.
'To hit the ceiling' (or hit the roof) means to become suddenly and violently angry. All the literal options about jumping or breaking a roof miss the figurative sense.
'Give up the ghost' means to die (the 'ghost' being the spirit leaving the body); by extension a machine that stops working is also said to give up the ghost.
'Go haywire' means to go out of control or stop functioning properly, from the tangled wire used to bale hay. The hay-related options play on that literal origin.
'On a par (with)' means equal in level or quality, of the same standard. 'Agree with someone' confuses it with 'on the same page'.

'Right and left' means on all sides, in every direction, usually of something happening abundantly (e.g. 'he was borrowing money right and left'). It has nothing to do with marching or direction-drill.

A capital crime is an offence for which the punishment may be death ('capital' from Latin caput, the head one loses). Option (d), 'death sentence', names capital punishment itself, not the crime, so it is the classic trap here.
A close-fisted (or tight-fisted) man keeps his fist closed over his money, i.e. he is stingy — a miser. The fist image tempts readers towards anger or fighting.
'Out of sorts' means slightly unwell or off-colour. Irritability is only a secondary shade of the phrase, so 'unwell' is the standard meaning tested.
Serene means peaceful, untroubled and tranquil — hence 'calm'. It describes both weather and temperament.
To abridge is to cut a text or right down to a shorter form, so 'shorten' is the synonym; an abridged edition is a condensed one.
Bashful means timid and easily embarrassed in company, i.e. shy; it comes from the same root as 'abash'.
Besides its political sense, liberal means free in giving — open-handed, hence 'generous' ('a liberal donation').
Diligent means hard-working and careful in one's duties, which is exactly what industrious means.
Handy means convenient and ready to use, i.e. useful. 'Bulky' is its practical opposite, since a bulky thing is awkward to handle.
Judicious means showing sound judgement, which is what prudent means. Note that judicious is about wisdom, not about courts — 'judicial' is the legal word.
Latent means present but not yet visible or active — hidden or dormant, as in 'latent talent' or 'latent heat'.
Ludicrous means so absurd as to invite ridicule, i.e. laughable (from Latin ludere, to play).
To repress is to hold back or subdue by force, and to stifle is likewise to smother or suppress — the two match closely.
A teetotaller is a person who abstains completely from alcoholic drink. The other options describe a nomad, a refugee/fugitive and a hedonist.
Acoustics is the science of sound and how it behaves in a space; 'acoustic' relates to sound and hearing. The science of antiquities is archaeology.

A coup d'etat (printed here without the apostrophe) is a sudden illegal or violent seizure of power from a government. A combination of states or parties is a coalition, and the ridiculing composition is a satire or lampoon.
Espionage is the practice of spying to obtain secret information. The engagement to marry is espousal/betrothal — the near-look-alike that makes this question work.
A creche is a day nursery where babies and small children are looked after while their parents work. The place where milk is kept is a dairy; the store for goods is a warehouse.
An arc is any continuous portion of the circumference of a circle or curve. Option (b), 'a ship', is the trap for the homophone 'ark'.

A curator is the keeper or officer in charge of a museum, art gallery or collection (Latin curare, to take care of). One who studies weather is a meteorologist; one who compiles dictionaries is a lexicographer.
Phonetics is the branch of linguistics dealing with speech sounds and how they are produced, transmitted and perceived. The study of metals is metallurgy and the study of pottery is ceramics.
A eulogy is a speech or piece of writing in high praise of someone, typically one who has died. An exaggerated statement is hyperbole and the concluding part of a work is the epilogue.
'Draw near' means to come closer or approach, whether in space or in time — here death is approaching. 'Withdraw' reverses the sense of the phrasal verb.
'Come to light' means to be revealed or become publicly known, which is exactly what an investigation does to hidden events.
'Beat about the bush' means to avoid the main point and speak in a roundabout way; it comes from hunters thrashing the undergrowth instead of catching the bird itself.
'Do without' means to manage or get along in the absence of something. The sentence therefore says they have learnt to manage without luxuries.
'In hot water' means in trouble or facing punishment for something one has done.
To 'give oneself airs' is to behave arrogantly, putting on a show of being superior or wealthier than one is — which is why the sentence adds that everyone knows she is broke.
'Hold one's own' means to maintain one's position successfully against opposition, i.e. not to be beaten — so 'to be defeated' is the exact opposite.
'Better half' is a humorous idiom for one's spouse, in standard usage the wife.
A close-fisted man is stingy — a miser — as the sentence itself confirms by saying he would rather starve than give anything away free.
'At daggers drawn' means openly hostile, on the point of fighting — bitter enemies. A truce would be the opposite state.
Conscious of something means aware of it. 'Oblivious' is its antonym, and 'suspicious' adds a shade of doubt that 'conscious' does not carry.
A reclusive person withdraws from company and lives in seclusion, so 'avoiding society' is the nearest meaning.
Invincible means incapable of being conquered — undefeatable. 'Invisible' is the near-look-alike trap, and it means unable to be seen.
Inevitable means certain to happen and impossible to avoid, i.e. unavoidable — the near-opposite of 'impossible'.
Apathy is absence of feeling or interest, i.e. indifference. Sympathy and empathy are the deliberate traps — they mean fellow-feeling, the opposite of apathy.
Candid means open and truthful, so its opposite is 'dishonest'. Option (a), 'frank', is a synonym and the standard trap in an antonym question.
Pompous means self-important and grandly boastful, so 'humble' is the opposite; 'proud' and 'boastful' are synonyms planted as traps.
Credible means believable or worthy of belief, so its antonym is 'unbelievable'; 'believable' is the synonym trap.
Inaccessible means impossible to reach, so the opposite is 'approachable'. 'Unapproachable' merely repeats the same idea.
Genuine means real and sincere, so 'fake' is its opposite; 'real' and 'truthful' are synonyms included to catch careless reading of the instruction.
Espionage is the practice of spying or of using spies to obtain secret information. 'An engagement to marry' is espousal, the look-alike distractor.
A linguist is a person skilled in several languages (or a student of language itself). A stamp-collector is a philatelist.
A philanderer is a man who carries on flirtations or love affairs with many women. The generous contributor is a philanthropist — the deliberately similar-sounding trap.
Utopia is an imaginary place where everything is perfect, from Sir Thomas More's book; its opposite is a dystopia.
Simultaneous describes events occurring at the same time (Latin simul, together) — as in simultaneous translation.
Oblivious means unaware of or not noticing what is happening around one. Inability to pay debts is insolvency.
Incorrigible means beyond correction or reform (in- + corrigere, to correct), used of habits and of people. 'Cannot be corrupted' is incorruptible — the near-look-alike trap.
A precedent is an earlier case or decision taken as a guide for later similar ones, a sense central to law. The ruler of a country is the president — the spelling trap here.
A bigot is someone obstinately intolerant of those with different beliefs or opinions. One who denies God is an atheist.
A conclusion is the end or finish of an event, process or piece of writing (it also means an inference drawn). 'To find out something' describes discovery, not conclusion.
'To drive home' means to make a point forcefully clear so that it is fully understood — to emphasise it. The literal 'return home' readings are the traps.

'To cry wolf' means to raise a false alarm repeatedly, so that a genuine warning is later ignored — from Aesop's shepherd boy. Option (d) is printed with a stray bracket, but that does not affect the answer.

In 'One half of this task', the word 'half' is the head of the phrase and is followed by 'of' — it is being used as a noun (compare 'half the task', where it is an adjective/determiner). The printed direction, 'Fill in the blanks', does not match the question, which actually asks for the part of speech of the underlined word.

'Fast' tells how one walks, which makes it an adverb of manner. The sentence is defective for this exercise because it contains a second adverb, 'so', which modifies 'fast' and is an adverb of degree, so option (b) is also defensible depending on which word the examiner underlined.
'Before' answers the question 'when?' — it places the hearing at some earlier time — so it is an adverb of time.
'Always' answers 'how often?', which is the test for an adverb of frequency (always, often, never, seldom, twice).
'Out' answers 'where?' — it states where the brother is — so it is an adverb of place.

'Never' answers 'how often?' (never = not on any occasion), so under the Wren & Martin scheme used by this paper it is an adverb of frequency. Some grammars file 'never' under adverbs of time, which makes option (d) arguable.

'Up to now' links a past action to the present moment and therefore demands the present perfect, 'have sent'. Note the stem is misprinted — 'only one better' is evidently meant to read 'only one letter' — but the time marker still fixes the tense.
A scheduled or timetabled future event takes the simple present: 'My uncle arrives tomorrow.' The perfect and past-continuous forms cannot combine with 'tomorrow'.

The present continuous is used for a fixed personal arrangement in the future, so 'She is playing in the concert tomorrow evening' is correct; the three perfect forms all refer to past time and clash with 'tomorrow'.
'Today' is an unfinished time period, so the present perfect 'have done' is required. 'Has done' is wrong in person, and 'did' would need a finished past time.
'Wherever you like' modifies the verb 'may sit' by telling where, so it is an adverb clause of place.
'Till I return' tells when the waiting is to continue, modifying the verb 'wait', so it is an adverb clause of time.
'That the weather will change' is the object of the verb 'predict' — it does the work of a noun — so it is a noun clause.
'Who comes late' qualifies the noun 'boy', doing the work of an adjective, so it is an adjective (relative) clause.
'Where I am' modifies the verb 'shall remain' by telling where, making it an adverb clause of place.

The established collective noun is a sheaf of wheat (or of corn) — the bundle of stalks tied after reaping. 'Bundle' and 'stack' are loosely possible in ordinary speech but 'sheaf' is the fixed term tested.
A group of cubs (or puppies or kittens) born together is a litter. A pack is used of adult wolves or hounds and a herd of grazing animals.

To laud is to praise highly, so 'praise' matches it directly in both form and sense. The question is loosely set: 'eulogy' (a noun for a speech of praise) and 'extolled' (a past-tense verb) also carry the idea of praising, but neither substitutes for 'laud' as cleanly as 'praise' does.
Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy, so 'hyperactive' is the antonym. 'Immobile' is the trap — being motionless is close to lethargy, not its opposite.
Latin 'per centum' literally means 'by the hundred', which is why a percentage expresses a quantity out of 100. 'Per annum' is per year and 'per se' is by itself.
